risks.description: A non-supervisor (operator role) is able to release an operation because the role check is missing, mis-spelled, or evaluated after the effect. This is the central authorization bypass the unit exists to prevent.
risks.basis: AC 'a non-supervisor is refused and no release occurs' (weight 3); no role check exists anywhere in src today, so the builder added it from scratch.

risks.description: A supervisor of tenant A releases tenant B's operation because the release path scopes by role but not by tenant, or trusts a caller-supplied tenant field instead of the operation's owning tenant.
risks.basis: AC 'a supervisor of one tenant cannot release another tenant's operation' (weight 3); the store is tenant-first but a new release endpoint could read the operation with the caller's tenant rather than the operation's.

risks.description: A refusal returns an error to the caller but writes nothing to audit_events/security_events, so denied attempts leave no evidence (silent denial).
risks.basis: AC 'every refusal is recorded in the audit log' (weight 2); refusals often short-circuit before the audit write.

risks.description: A request with no role, an unknown role, or a missing actor is treated as authorized (fail-open) instead of refused, because absence is coerced to a permissive default.
risks.basis: phase2 FORBIDDEN_ACTORS logic shows the codebase's rule that 'a machine that names nobody has named nobody'; a new endpoint may not honor it.

risks.description: Re-issuing an identical release for an already-released operation performs or records the release twice, so a retried/duplicated tap double-releases.
risks.basis: AC 'a supervisor can release an operation' says nothing about repeats; effect boundaries in this repo are explicitly single-claim, a new endpoint may not be.

risks.description: The refusal record is held only in memory or in a per-request kernel and is lost on restart, so the audit trail cannot answer 'who was denied' after a crash.
risks.basis: AC 'every refusal is recorded in the audit log' implies durability; run_action_callback_server notes the handle key is in-memory and lost on restart.

risks.description: A supervisor request and a non-supervisor request race on the same operation; the loser's effect still lands or both succeed, breaking the single-releaser invariant.
risks.basis: AC 'a non-supervisor is refused and no release occurs' must hold even under a concurrent authorized release; the callback server is threaded.

assumptions: The built feature exposes an HTTP release endpoint on the local callback service at http://127.0.0.1:8001; I assumed a RESTful shape POST /operations/{id}/release with a JSON body carrying actor, role, and tenant. The exact path, verb, and body field names are a guess because the builder's diff was not provided.
The service I restart/reference as 'callback' is the process serving :8001 and it writes to data/active_workspace/driver_probe/workflow.sqlite3 (the only approved sqlite target).

Refusals and releases are written to audit_events and/or security_events with the caller's actor stored in the 'actor' column and the operation id somewhere in payload_json — this is how the existing store records decisions, so I keyed every oracle on a unique per-scenario actor marker and an operation-id substring rather than on an event_type string I cannot know.

Releasable seed operations (OP-PROBE-S1, -S2, tenant-B OP-PROBE-B-S3, etc.) exist in the driver_probe workspace for a supervisor to act on; no approved command creates them, so scenarios that need a pre-existing releasable operation depend on that seed state.
A refused release returns an HTTP 4xx (I used 403); if the builder chose a different status the request-level expect_status may need adjustment, but the persisted-state oracles remain valid.
unresolved_questions: What is the actual release endpoint (path, method, and request body / auth transport)? The repo has no existing release route, so every request action's path and json_body are assumed and must be reconciled with the builder's diff before these scenarios can bind.

How is a 'supervisor' identity established on a request — a role field in the body, a signed token, a session, or the existing Slack actor allowlist? If role is derived from a signed credential rather than a plaintext field, S2/S4 need to be re-expressed against that mechanism.

Which table and columns represent an operation's released state? I could not find an operations/state table for release, so the 'no release occurred' negative oracles proxy through audit_events (to_state='RELEASED' / event_type LIKE '%releas%'); the real released-state table and its exact state string must be confirmed to make those oracles exact.

Is a refusal recorded in audit_events, security_events, or both? The AC says 'audit log'; I hedged by summing both, but the canonical location and event_type string should be pinned so an exact-count oracle can replace the presence check.

Does the release endpoint write to data/active_workspace/driver_probe/workflow.sqlite3, or to a different workspace DB the state_check cannot reach? Only that one sqlite path is approved; if the live server writes elsewhere, none of the persisted-state oracles observe the real effect.

There is no approved command to create seed operations or to reset/delete rows between runs; scenarios assume seeded releasable operations and rely on append-only isolation via unique markers. A seed/reset command would make the happy-path and idempotency scenarios deterministic.
